criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community domestic/drinking water access alongside agricultural irrigation and commercial urban water supply in peri-urban Kathmandu Valley (specifically in Jhaukhel, covering metered piped drinking water, community-managed drinking water schemes, household borewells/dugwells, public stone spouts, and household dependence on commercial water factories and tanker vendors when public supply is absent or irregular; Dadhikot focuses primarily on canal irrigation alongside community drinking-water schemes and household wells).
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the study examines statutory, customary, and institutional water governance (1992 Water Resources Act, 2012 Groundwater Policy, Kathmandu Valley Water Supply Management Board [KVWSMB], VDC governance, and customary water rights). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it directly examines rule-type mechanisms governing domestic and urban water access: (1) administrative discretion and regulatory non-enforcement/forbearance by KVWSMB and local VDC authorities toward illegal/unpermitted commercial extraction of shallow aquifers reserved for domestic use and deep-aquifer permitting rules; (2) overlapping licensing and registration rules across KVWSMB, the Department of Cottage and Small Industries, and municipal tax collection governing commercial water suppliers/vendors; and (3) de facto land-tenure/ownership requirements conditioning rights to drill wells and access groundwater (as well as maintenance-contribution rules in Dadhikot).
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary qualitative socio-legal empirical evidence from an ethnographic comparative case study conducted in 2015-2016 in two peri-urban VDCs (Dadhikot and Jhaukhel), comprising semistructured and informal interviews, focus group discussions, field observations, and policy document review.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports qualitative household and community access outcomes, including drying of household borewells, shallow wells, and stone spouts; irregular piped supply; women's queuing burden, exclusion (returning empty-handed), and receipt of poor-quality unfiltered water when fetching drinking water from commercial water factories; household water purchasing and precarious dependence on commercial water vendors; and declining irrigation water availability.
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies the population and units of analysis (households, women water fetchers, ancestral/inmigrant/tenant farmers, commercial water factories/vendors, brick kiln operators, and government officials across two peri-urban VDCs in Kathmandu Valley), the legal/regulatory/tenure exposures, the water access/reliability/exclusion outcomes, and the qualitative ethnographic case study design.

evidence_quotes.quote: Field research was carried out by the first author in 2015 and 2016. The research was designed as an ethnographic case study (LeCompte and Schensul 2010).

Public and private groundwater use is increasing with unplanned urban expansion, while the growing urban demand, which is not satisfied by public water provision, creates among authorities an attitude characterized by discretion and nonintervention rather than strict enforcement.

A piped drinking water supply system started functioning in 1993 and extended its service to households through a metered tap connection by 1994. With increasing settlement, water demands rose while supply turned irregular. Over the years, community-managed drinking water systems emerged and expanded in various hamlets.

The Kathmandu Valley Water Supply Management Board admitted in an interview that, contradicting the groundwater policy, shallow aquifers are commercially used. Nonetheless, KVWSMB limits its interventions because commercial water suppliers are important in filling the increasing gaps between urban water demand and supplies. Thus, commercial water users gain legal access to water through overlapping and weak government registration.

Since then we are fetching water from water factories. Even if these factory people hesitate and shout at us, we do not have other options. It is mostly women who do this job. If we do not succeed at one factory we try another. Sometimes we return empty-handed or with water that turns yellow in a day, they are reluctant to give filtered water.

After drying up of their water sources, Jhaukhel residents depend on water vendors, despite the fact that the former have water rights and the latter’s practices are illegal. This shows that water access is not always rights-based, nor do rights always ensure access (see Ribot and Peluso 2003). Notwithstanding the existence of a governmental permit system for commercial exploitation of deep aquifers and a prohibition of commercial exploitation of shallow ones, transgressions of both are tolerated because of the urgency of urban water provision.

raw_response.exposure: Legal-pluralist water rights, de facto land-tenure requirements for groundwater access, overlapping industrial versus water-authority registration/permitting rules, and regulatory discretion/non-enforcement by KVWSMB and local VDC authorities under the 1992 Water Resources Act and 2012 Groundwater Policy (alongside customary canal maintenance rules in Dadhikot).
raw_response.outcome: Household domestic and drinking water availability, continuity, and exclusion (drying of household wells and public spouts, irregular piped water, women returning empty-handed or receiving unfiltered water from commercial factories, water purchasing, and precarious household dependence on commercial water vendors), as well as irrigation water access.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Peri-urban residents/households (including women fetching domestic water and ancestral/inmigrant/tenant farmers), commercial water vendors/factory owners, brick factory operators, and government officials in two peri-urban VDCs (Dadhikot and Jhaukhel) in Kathmandu Valley, Nepal (Dadhikot: 38 informal talks/interviews, 17 open/semistructured interviews, 3 FGDs; Jhaukhel: 39 informal talks/interviews, 30 open/semistructured interviews, 3 FGDs; plus 26 government official interviews; units of analysis: household, user group, and community).
raw_response.rationale: Full-text ethnographic socio-legal study in peri-urban Kathmandu Valley, Nepal, meeting all inclusion criteria under both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings of Criterion 2. Although the Dadhikot case focuses mainly on agricultural irrigation canals, the Jhaukhel case directly investigates household drinking/domestic water access and commercial urban water supply, showing how land-tenure-based groundwater claims, overlapping business vs. water-board registration/permitting rules, and explicit regulatory discretion and non-enforcement of the 2012 Groundwater Policy by KVWSMB and the VDC lead to depletion of household wells/spouts, exclusion of women seeking drinking water, and household dependence on commercial water factories and vendors. Qualitative socio-legal studies with identifiable empirical methods are eligible for the systematic review's mechanism synthesis.
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative ethnographic comparative case study (two peri-urban sites, fieldwork in 2015-2016 using semistructured and informal interviews, focus group discussions, field observations, and policy document analysis)
